common_name: Prince Charles Clematis (Compact Sky-Blue Viticella-Type Clematis)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded while the vine climbs into full sun to light shade; a compact, free-flowering cultivar suited to a smaller trellis or large container.

directions: Plant with roots shaded and cool while the vine climbs into full sun to light shade. Prince Charles bears a profusion of medium-sized, clear sky-blue flowers with a light central boss of cream stamens over a long bloom period from early summer into fall, flowering on new growth so it can be pruned back hard each late winter along with other pruning-group-three clematis. Its moderate size and exceptionally free-flowering habit make it a good choice for a large container on a patio trellis or a smaller garden obelisk where a more rampant clematis would quickly outgrow the space. Water regularly during the growing season and mulch to keep roots cool, since clematis generally prefer shaded roots with their foliage reaching into the sun.

common_name: Kardynal Wyszynski Clematis (Deep Purple-Blue Large-Flowered Clematis)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded while the vine climbs into full sun to light shade; a vigorous Polish-bred large-flowered clematis.

directions: Plant with roots shaded and cool while the vine climbs into full sun to light shade. Kardynal Wyszynski bears large, deep purple-blue flowers with a velvety texture and a contrasting boss of cream to yellow stamens, produced heavily in early summer with a lighter repeat flush later in the season. Named for the Polish cardinal, it is a vigorous grower well suited to a substantial trellis, arbor, or fence where its rich color can be shown off against a light-colored wall or dark evergreen backdrop. Water regularly during the growing season and mulch to keep roots cool, and prune according to its bloom-on-old-and-new-wood habit, removing only dead or weak growth in late winter to preserve the bulk of the early flush.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded while the vine climbs into full sun to light shade; blooms over a long season from midsummer into fall.

directions: Plant with roots shaded and cool while the vine climbs into full sun to light shade. Rhapsody bears rich, deep blue flowers with a slightly ruffled edge and a contrasting cream center of stamens, flowering on new growth over an extended season from midsummer well into fall, which lets it be pruned back hard each late winter along with other pruning-group-three clematis. Its saturated, true-blue color is a useful complement to the more common purples, pinks, and whites in a mixed clematis collection trained along a fence or trellis. Water regularly during the growing season and mulch to keep roots cool, since clematis generally prefer shaded roots with their foliage reaching into the sun.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; part of the compact Raymond Evison Patio series bred specifically for container growing.

directions: Plant with roots shaded and cool while the vine climbs into full sun to light shade. Cezanne bears rounded, china-blue flowers with a contrasting center of cream stamens on a compact plant bred specifically for container culture, reaching only a few feet tall on a small trellis or obelisk rather than sprawling the ten feet or more typical of vigorous climbing clematis. Its manageable size makes it a good choice for a patio pot, balcony rail planter, or small garden space where a full-sized clematis would be impractical. Water container-grown plants more frequently than those in the ground, since pots dry out faster, and mulch the soil surface to keep roots cool and shaded.

common_name: Fireworks Clematis (Purple-Blue Large-Flowered Clematis with Red-Purple Bar)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded while the vine climbs into full sun to light shade; a long-popular bicolor large-flowered clematis.

directions: Plant with roots shaded and cool while the vine climbs into full sun to light shade. Fireworks bears large, twisted, star-like flowers in violet-blue with a bold reddish-purple central bar down each petal, a striking bicolor pattern radiating outward from the yellow-stamened center that gives the cultivar its explosive namesake look. It flowers heavily in late spring to early summer with a lighter repeat bloom later in the season on a vigorous vine well suited to a substantial trellis, arbor, or fence. Water regularly during the growing season and mulch to keep roots cool, and prune lightly after the first flush to tidy growth while preserving buds for the later repeat bloom.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; unlike most clematis, Arabella has a scrambling, non-clinging habit and works as well sprawling through a border as it does trained on a support.

directions: Plant with roots shaded and cool while the foliage grows into full sun to light shade. Arabella is a non-vining, shrub-like integrifolia-type clematis that produces a long, prolific succession of nodding, star-shaped blue-purple flowers with prominent cream stamens from early summer well into fall, without needing a strong climbing structure since it lacks the twining leaf-petioles of vining clematis types. Its low, mounding, spreading habit lets it be used as a border filler, allowed to scramble through a low shrub, or grown up a small support if a more upright look is wanted. It flowers entirely on new growth, so cutting the whole plant back hard in late winter each year keeps it tidy and promotes the heaviest bloom. Water regularly during the growing season and mulch to keep roots cool.

common_name: Sweet Summer Love Clematis (Vigorous Fragrant Reddish-Purple Clematis)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded while the vine climbs into full sun to light shade; bred as a fragrant, more compact, non-invasive alternative to sweet autumn clematis.

directions: Plant with roots shaded and cool while the vine climbs into full sun to light shade. Sweet Summer Love smothers itself in masses of small, star-shaped, richly fragrant reddish-purple flowers from mid to late summer into fall, bred as a sterile, non-seeding, better-behaved alternative to the sometimes weedy sweet autumn clematis while keeping a similarly vigorous, heavy-blooming habit. It climbs eagerly onto a substantial arbor, fence, or trellis, and its late-season bloom fills a gap after most large-flowered clematis have finished for the year. Because it flowers on new growth, cut it back hard in late winter to keep it in bounds and to encourage the heaviest late-summer flush. Water regularly during the growing season and mulch to keep roots cool.

common_name: Stand By Me Clematis (Non-Vining Upright Indigo-Blue Shrub Clematis)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun to light shade; a non-vining, upright clematis that can be grown in a perennial border without any climbing support.

directions: Plant with roots shaded and cool in full sun to light shade. Stand By Me is a shrubby, non-climbing clematis that grows as an upright perennial rather than a vine, producing nodding, bell-shaped indigo-blue flowers with slightly recurved petal tips over a long bloom season from early summer into fall, all without needing a trellis or other climbing support. Its self-supporting habit makes it uniquely useful for a mixed perennial border or large container where a typical vining clematis would need staking or a structure to climb. It flowers on new growth, so cutting the whole plant back to the ground in late winter keeps it tidy and encourages a strong flush the following season. Water regularly during the growing season and mulch to keep roots cool.

common_name: Sugar Candy Clematis (Pale Mauve-Pink Large-Flowered Clematis with Darker Bar)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded while the vine climbs into full sun to light shade; a compact, free-flowering cultivar suited to a smaller trellis or large container.

directions: Plant with roots shaded and cool while the vine climbs into full sun to light shade. Sugar Candy bears pale mauve-pink flowers with a deeper pink-purple bar running down the center of each petal, a soft two-tone pattern that reads as gentle and pastel from a distance but shows fine detail up close. Its moderate size and compact growth suit a smaller trellis, obelisk, or large patio container as well as a spot in the open border trained onto a nearby shrub. Water regularly during the growing season and mulch to keep roots cool, and prune lightly to shape after the main flush of bloom while leaving enough growth for a repeat show later in the season.

common_name: Sally Coates Clematis (White Large-Flowered Clematis with Mauve-Pink Bar)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded while the vine climbs into full sun to light shade.

directions: Plant with roots shaded and cool while the vine climbs into full sun to light shade. Sally Coates bears large, overlapping white flowers washed with a soft mauve-pink bar down the center of each petal and a center of contrasting stamens, a delicate bicolor combination that reads as nearly white from a distance but shows subtle color up close. It blooms heavily in late spring to early summer with a repeat flush later in the season on a vigorous vine suited to a substantial trellis, arbor, or fence. Water regularly during the growing season and mulch to keep roots cool, and prune lightly after the first flush to tidy growth while preserving buds for the later repeat bloom.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded while the vine climbs into full sun to light shade; part of the Raymond Evison double-flowered breeding line.

directions: Plant with roots shaded and cool while the vine climbs into full sun to light shade. Diamantina bears fully double, heavily ruffled purple-blue flowers resembling a dahlia or peony more than a typical single-layer clematis bloom, opening double on the first early-summer flush and often shifting to a simpler single form on the smaller repeat bloom later in the season, a trait shared by other double clematis cultivars. Its unusual, frilly flower form makes it a conversation piece trained on a trellis, obelisk, or large container support near a patio where the intricate blooms can be appreciated up close. Water regularly during the growing season and mulch to keep roots cool, and prune lightly to preserve old wood if the strongest double flowers are wanted the following year.
